name: ST Math
line: ST Math teaches with visual puzzles in a fixed order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs ST Math: ST Math teaches through visual puzzles in a fixed sequence. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: ST Math teaches through visual puzzles in a fixed sequence, one grade's Journey at a time, and for a stuck student MIND's guide turns to an adult [3][5][7]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. We found no placement test in ST Math: a student starts on the Journey for their grade [7], and the sequence is fixed, taken at the student's own pace [3]. In the full program, each objective from grade 2 opens and closes with a quiz, and students move on whatever their post-quiz score [9].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In ST Math the teaching is the puzzle itself, concepts before symbols [1]. We found no hints in the software. For a stuck student, MIND's guide turns to an adult's questions, hands-on materials and a few in-game tools, and says not to give the answer [5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [27].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In ST Math an animation shows what the answer does: the penguin JiJi gets across or does not [3][22]. The authors of the independent trial noted that every student who picks the same wrong answer sees the same animation [11]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [26].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once. AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, and repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In ST Math the next level opens when every puzzle in a level is right. Two wrong answers restart the level, until 15 tries on it turn the restart off [3][8]. MIND recommends keeping a student on their assigned grade, and moving to an earlier grade is a step the adult takes [6][23]. In the independent trial, students with the lowest starting scores finished under half their grade's content, and the authors suggested they may have needed work from earlier grades [11].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In ST Math, topics come back where the fixed sequence spirals to them [3]. Mixed Review is bonus content after the Journey [10], and the streamlined ST Math Focus leaves it out [4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [25].

rows.range: PreK through grade 8, as a supplemental program [1][3].
rows.start: No placement test found in the pages we read. A student starts on the Journey for their grade [7].
rows.teaching: Visual, mostly wordless puzzles. An animation shows what each answer does [3][22]. For a stuck student, MIND's guide turns to an adult [5].
rows.next: A fixed sequence, at the student's own pace [3]. An adult can assign objectives from any grade [21].
rows.mastery: Every puzzle in a level right. Two wrong answers restart the level, until 15 tries turn the restart off [3][8]. Students move on whatever their post-quiz score [9].
rows.review: Topics spiral back in the fixed sequence [3]. Mixed Review is bonus content after the Journey [10].
rows.print: Printable Math Mats and classroom sheets, many in Spanish [5][17]. The only workbooks we found are fixed ones for the Texas edition [20].
rows.adult: In MIND's guides, the adult coaches a stuck student with questions and hands-on materials, and moves a student to an earlier grade by hand [5][6][23].
rows.reports: Parents: objectives, puzzle goals and quiz scores [18]. Teachers: minutes, puzzles per minute and alerts on students [19][8].
rows.evidence: Rated Strong by Evidence for ESSA, average +0.07 [2]. One independent randomized trial: 0.07 SD after a year, marginally significant [11].

theirs: ST Math is made by MIND Education, a nonprofit founded in 1998 [24]. MIND describes it as a PreK to grade 8 supplemental math program, built on "concepts before symbols": a student meets an idea in a visual puzzle before its symbols [1][3]. In schools, class discussions MIND calls Math Puzzle Talks help students explain what they learned [1].

A student opens the Journey for their grade, a map of objectives. Each objective holds games, and each game holds levels of 5 to 8 puzzles [7][22]. A puzzle is a visual, mostly wordless problem: JiJi the penguin is blocked, the student moves objects such as fraction blocks or a number line, and an animation shows whether JiJi gets across [3][22][11]. In the full program, objectives from grade 2 open and close with a quiz [9].
credit: Visual models a learner moves, such as number lines and fraction blocks [3][22]. A What Works Clearinghouse guide for elementary math intervention rates the evidence for such representations, and for the number line, as strong [28].
Puzzles designed to work without words [3].
An independent randomized trial in 52 schools, funded by the U.S. Institute of Education Sciences [11][13].

theirs: Evidence for ESSA rates ST Math Strong for grades 3 to 6, on four studies with an average effect of +0.07 [2]. One is an independent randomized trial. The other three were written by MIND or done by WestEd under contract to MIND [2][14][15]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report for ST Math [29].

The trial, by Rutherford and colleagues (2014), was run by independent researchers without oversight from MIND and funded by a U.S. Institute of Education Sciences grant [11][13]. It randomized 52 low-performing Southern California schools, and its analysis covered 13,803 students in grades 3 to 5. Classes in ST Math schools were scheduled for two 45-minute sessions a week. After one year the effect on the state math test was 0.07 standard deviations, marginally significant. After two years it was 0.15 and not significant. The abstract calls the effect on math scores negligible [11][12]. English learners and students with the lowest starting scores gained no more than other students [11].

WestEd's 2019 study, prepared under contract to MIND, compared grades in 474 schools across 16 states that adopted ST Math with similar grades that did not. It found 0.13 on scale scores and 0.17 on percent proficient. Both are measured against the spread of school-grade averages rather than of students, so they are not on the same scale as the trial's 0.07. WestEd notes that districts which chose the program may have differed in other ways [14]. A non-experimental Harvard study from 2020, in 13 school systems, compared students whose weekly use rose by more than 10 minutes with similar students whose use stayed flat, and found close to 0.04 standard deviations. In grades 2 to 5, students averaged 49 minutes a week against a recommended 90 [16].
ours: The two findings that bear most on this comparison: across 55 studies, worked examples improved math performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [27], and across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for right or wrong alone [26]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is not yet reading, and you want first math as visual puzzles without words.
amp: You want the teaching on the screen at every problem: a hint, a lesson and the worked answer.
You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate quizzes.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is past grade 8, or soon will be.

questions.question: How is AMP different from ST Math?
questions.answer: ST Math teaches through visual puzzles in a fixed sequence, and for a stuck student MIND's guide turns to an adult [3][5]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does ST Math work?
questions.answer: Its independent randomized trial found 0.07 standard deviations on the state math test after one year, marginally significant, and no significant effect after two [11]. Evidence for ESSA rates it Strong, on four studies with an average effect of +0.07 [2].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
